concepts.title: The Versatile Nature of Carbon - Covalent Bonding

questions.q: Why is carbon's covalency called tetravalency?
questions.a: One carbon atom forms four covalent bonds by sharing its four outer electrons.

questions.q: Why does carbon show the property of catenation?
questions.a: C-C bonds are strong and stable, so carbon atoms link into long chains and rings.

questions.q: Why are there so many carbon compounds in nature?
questions.a: Tetravalency plus catenation lets carbon build chains, branches and rings with many elements - millions of compounds.

concepts.title: Hydrocarbons, Functional Groups and Homologous Series

questions.a: A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula where successive members differ by CH2 (14 u).

questions.q: Give the general formulae of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
questions.a: Alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2.

questions.q: Name the functional groups of alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids.

concepts.title: Chemical Properties and Reactions of Carbon Compounds

questions.q: What happens when ethyl alcohol burns in air?
questions.a: It burns with a clean blue flame forming CO2 and water, releasing heat - a combustion reaction.

questions.q: Which reaction turns ethanol into ethene?
questions.a: Dehydration with hot concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K removes water, giving ethene.

questions.q: What is the reaction between ethanol and ethanoic acid called and what is the product?
questions.a: Esterification; the sweet ester ethyl ethanoate plus water form.

questions.q: Why is soap ineffective in hard water while detergent works?
questions.a: Soap forms insoluble scum with Ca/Mg ions; detergents avoid this and clean in hard water.

questions.q: Explain the term 'micelle' in soap action.
questions.a: A cluster where soap tails trap the oil droplet inside and heads face the water, letting the oil be rinsed away.

questions.q: Why are carbonaceous fuels called hydrocarbons?
questions.a: They contain only hydrogen and carbon, which burn to give CO2, water and heat.
